strengths: Clear identification of the core problem: MLLMs fail to attend to safety-critical image regions, supported by compelling evidence (Figures 1, 3-4) with FDR analysis quantifying representational separability
Well-motivated three-stage design where each component addresses a specific failure mode with principled separation of risk evaluation (on reformulated queries) from steering (on original queries)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 models and multiple benchmarks (MM-SafetyBench, SPA-VL, FigStep, Sci-QA, MM-Vet, GQA, MME) showing strong ASR reductions (89.5% average) while maintaining original utility and improving inference throughput
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating contribution of each component and robustness to design choices (hyperparameter sensitivity, alternative prototype sources)
Strong attention to reproducibility with clearly reported hyperparameters, implementation details, public benchmarks, and code release commitment
Practical efficiency advantages over iterative refinement methods (ECSO, ETA) by steering only first 3 tokens at last layer
Generalization across diverse models and architectures without retraining
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: query reformulation with visual summaries is straightforward, prototype-based similarity evaluation is standard, and activation steering directly adapts existing work (Arditi et al. 2024). The contribution is primarily in combining techniques rather than methodological innovation

Critical robustness gap: visual context generation in Stage 1 could be adversarially targeted but receives no analysis. No evaluation of whether visual contexts are reliable or how generation failures affect the defense

Model-specific hyperparameter tuning undermines generalizability: Sbase and α require per-model calibration from safety data (α ranges 3.5× across models in Table 3), requiring practitioners to obtain calibration data at deployment

Unjustified cross-query steering design: risk is evaluated on reformulated queries (with visual context + safety prompt) but applied to steering of original queries (without augmentations). This mismatch is never explicitly justified theoretically

Insufficient adversarial robustness analysis: no evaluation against adaptive attacks, no study of visual context adversarial manipulation, no analysis of distribution shift between calibration and deployment

Limited problem analysis scope: FDR computed on simple object discrimination (bombs vs. chairs) but applied to complex jailbreaks (drug manufacturing, weapons trafficking). No validation that simple object FDR predicts complex scenario safety

Experimental design choices lack justification: choice of 50 unsafe text queries for prototypes not validated, exponential decay in Eq. 4 not compared to alternatives, N=3 chosen empirically without principled basis

Incomplete baseline comparisons: no comparison to training-based safety methods mentioned in related work (SPA-VL, DREAM), no comparison to naturally-safe models, missing detailed analysis of why RAS outperforms the strongest baseline (ETA)

Limited safety evaluation scope: benchmarks focus on object-based and typographic attacks; missing evaluation on adversarial patches, semantic contradictions, role-play jailbreaks, and compositional attacks
Single-direction steering assumption may not capture multidimensional refusal behavior, with no analysis of direction generalization across attack types or ablation on vector definition choices

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: Figure 1 compellingly demonstrates that MLLMs ignore safety-critical visual content despite refusing similar text-only queries, providing clear motivation for the work

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple dimensions: diverse benchmarks (MM-SafetyBench, SPA-VL, FigStep, Sci-QA, MM-Vet, GQA, MME), multiple models (LLaVA-1.5-7B/13B, Qwen-VL-Chat, InternLM-XComposer), detailed ablations, and speed measurements
Strong empirical results: Substantially reduces attack success rates (2-6% across benchmarks) while maintaining utility and inference speed compared to state-of-the-art inference-time defenses
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-written with good visual intuition (Figures 2-3), detailed hyperparameters in appendices, and commitment to release code
Diverse evaluation showing generalization: Results consistent across multiple model architectures and attack types (object recognition, typographic, Stable Diffusion)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The approach primarily combines existing techniques—visual context addition (Pandey et al. 2022, Kang et al. 2025a/b), activation steering (Arditi et al. 2024), and prototype-based similarity—without significant algorithmic innovation or new conceptual insights

Circular logic in visual context generation: The method uses the target MLLM to generate visual contexts needed for its own safety. If the model can generate accurate descriptions of safety-critical content, the rationale for why it cannot use this capability to refuse without steering is unclear and potentially fragile to adversarial visual contexts

Insufficient and under-justified prototype construction: Unsafe prototypes built from only 50 GPT-4 queries and S_base determined from 100 SPA-VL samples—very small sets without justification for representativeness across diverse unsafe content types. Model-specific α values vary widely (10.2-35.3), suggesting instability

Arbitrary design choices lacking principled justification: Activation steering limited to last layer and first 3 tokens is computationally motivated but may miss safety-critical steering opportunities. Exponential weighting parameter γ=0.3 shows high sensitivity (Figure 8) with no principled derivation beyond empirical tradeoff

Incomplete safety evaluation: Uses only classifier-based metric (MD-Judge-v0.2-InternLM2) without human evaluation; no analysis of false positive/negative rates, no evaluation against adaptive attacks, no systematic failure case analysis; qualitative examples in Appendix H appear cherry-picked

Tenuous connection between FDR and safety: FDR improvement (Figures 3-4, 12) used to motivate Stage 1, but connection between higher FDR on specific object pairs and actual jailbreak safety is correlational, not causal. No evidence that improvements on ImageNet/Dangerous Objects transfer to evaluated attack types

Fragile method dependent on visual quality: Table 2 shows significant performance degradation without images, indicating brittle reliance on visual input quality and accurate visual encoding. No analysis of robustness to inaccurate or adversarially-crafted visual contexts

Limited evaluation scope and generalization concerns: Evaluated only on three attack types (objects, typography, SD). Unclear how method generalizes to other visual jailbreaks (adversarial patches, semantic manipulations), out-of-distribution images, or multimodal content beyond images
Missing adversarial robustness analysis: No evaluation against adaptive attacks designed to fool this specific defense or to generate misleading visual contexts. Critical for a safety mechanism

Theoretical gaps: No principled justification for why adaptive scaling by risk score (Eq. 7) should outperform threshold-based alternatives. Limited theoretical analysis of why the approach should work beyond empirical observation

strengths: Clear problem identification with compelling empirical evidence: The FDR analysis effectively quantifies insufficient cross-modal attention to safety-critical regions across query formulations
Well-motivated three-stage design: Each stage logically addresses distinct problems (attention gaps, distribution shifts, proportional intervention)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple models, safety benchmarks (MM-SafetyBench, SPA-VL, FigStep), utility benchmarks (Sci-QA, MM-Vet, GQA, MME), and thorough ablations
Substantial and consistent improvements: 89.5% average ASR reduction while maintaining perfect utility and improving inference speed across diverse models
Strong technical execution: Clear mathematical formulations, well-motivated exponential weighting for early tokens, reasonable risk mapping approach
High reproducibility: Detailed implementation details, specified hyperparameters, plans to release code, uses public benchmarks. Ablations on query sources show robustness
Excellent presentation: Informative figures (especially Figures 3-4 on attention maps and FDR), clear narrative flow, thorough appendices
weaknesses: Unclear computational cost of visual context generation: Stage 1 requires an additional forward pass through the model, but timing measurements in Figure 7 don't explicitly account for this. Throughput claims need clarification regarding what is included in measurements

Limited novelty in individual components: Visual context augmentation is straightforward; activation steering is from prior work (Arditi et al. 2024); exponential weighting is natural but not novel. Main contribution is in combination and adaptive scaling, which is somewhat incremental

Methodological dependency on external LLMs: Unsafe prototypes from GPT-4; calibration uses only 100 samples for Sbase/α; large model-specific variations in α (10-35, Table 3) indicate substantial per-model tuning requirements; while ablated, the principle is inelegant

Incomplete failure mode analysis: No discussion of attacks targeting visual context generation itself; unclear behavior on ambiguous queries; no analysis of adversarial approaches exploiting the known steering mechanism; limited out-of-distribution evaluation

Circular reasoning concern: Using the model to generate descriptions to improve the same model's safety reasoning. If vision-language alignment is fundamentally flawed, can it reliably describe safety-critical content? Potential failure modes not discussed
Limited practical generalization: Requires access to model internals (not applicable to black-box APIs); only tested on open-source models; fixed safety prompt not ablated for sensitivity analysis

Risk evaluation design choices not fully justified: Sigmoid function choice (Eq. 5) appears arbitrary with no ablation; calibration on 100 samples may not capture distribution properties; the method assumes well-defined safe/unsafe separation which may not hold universally

Evaluation limitations: ASR judged by MD-Judge (LLM-based evaluator with potential biases); benchmarks are standard without evaluation on novel emerging attacks; utility evaluation doesn't test most complex reasoning tasks that might be most sensitive to activation perturbations

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification with clear quantitative (FDR) and qualitative (attention maps) analysis showing insufficient cross-modal attention to safety-critical regions
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 diverse jailbreak benchmarks, 5 MLLM architectures, and both safety and utility metrics with detailed ablations and sensitivity analyses
Strong practical results: 19.4% ASR reduction, maintained utility, 126.6× less pre-deployment overhead, and good generalization across model architectures without per-model tuning

Technically sound three-stage pipeline design with logical motivation: addressing attention deficits → avoiding over-refusal through risk estimation → adaptive steering; query-adaptive refusal vectors outperform global vectors (Table 7)

Extensive supplementary material with reproducibility details, alternative calibration datasets, hyperparameter sensitivity, qualitative results, and rigorous baseline comparisons with hyperparameter search results
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: individual components (visual contexts [34-36], activation steering [23-25]) are established; core contribution is engineering-focused combination rather than methodological innovation

Causality claims in Section 3.1 rest on correlational evidence (low FDR → unsafe outputs) but lack rigorous causal proof; alternative explanations for safety failures not explored despite empirical fix working

Visual context generation relies on the MLLM itself (Algorithm 1 line 4), creating circularity: if the model has multimodal safety issues, can it reliably describe safety-critical regions? No failure mode analysis or adversarial robustness of this stage

Prototype-based approach (Eq. 2-3) uses mean activations and cosine similarity without justification; no comparison with alternative distance metrics or prototype definitions that might be more effective

Incomplete baseline comparison: AutoSteer/ASTRA required extensive hyperparameter tuning (Sec. 13) while MoRAS parameters (γ, N, α, Sb) claimed 'automatically determined' via calibration—creates potential comparison bias
Insufficient analysis of failure cases: VAA ASR remains 14.3% (notably higher than other benchmarks), yet no error analysis of when/why MoRAS fails or vulnerability to unconsidered attack types
Over-refusal trade-off underexplored: XSTest/OR-Bench show 3.2-4.3% increases; safety-utility frontier not analyzed despite being critical for deployment decisions

Evaluation limited to recent models (2024-2025); generalization to older/smaller models or different vision encoders unclear; ASR evaluation relies on single judge (MD-Judge-v0.2-Internlm2) introducing potential bias

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Empirically validates insufficient cross-modal attention to safety-critical image regions through FDR analysis and visualizations
Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple benchmarks (SPA-VL, FigStep, MM-Safety, JOOD, VAA), model architectures, both safety and utility metrics, with extensive supplementary ablations
Practical efficiency: 126.6× lower pre-deployment overhead (1.35 min vs 472.3 min for ASTRA) with minimal inference slowdown and utility preservation
Strong empirical results across diverse settings: Achieves 7.6% ASR on SPA-VL while maintaining vanilla utility levels across multiple MLLM architectures
Thorough supplementary materials: 13 supplementary sections including hyperparameter sensitivity, generalization studies, qualitative results, and baseline hyperparameter searches
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Visual context generation (prompting), unsafe prototypes (standard activation averaging), risk evaluation (cosine similarity + sigmoid), and activation steering (application of [23]) are all straightforward. The contribution is combining known components without fundamental innovation

Insufficient causal analysis: Paper shows MLLMs attend less to safety-critical regions but does not rigorously prove this causes safety failures. Alternative explanations (models learn text-only queries are safe; inherent vision-language misalignment) are unexplored. The causal claim rests primarily on correlation

Visual context as confounding factor: It is unclear whether improved safety comes from enhanced cross-modal attention, additional textual safety signals, or simply better prompt engineering. Visual context is MLLM-generated, raising questions about circular reasoning

Experimental methodology concerns: (1) LLM-based evaluation only (MD-Judge-v0.2)—no human evaluation of actual safety; (2) Potential hyperparameter tuning bias for baselines (Sec. 13) raises fairness questions; (3) Some baseline improvements suspicious (e.g., ASTRA: 27.2% on MM-Safety vs MoRAS: 2.6%), suggesting possible implementation issues

High variance across models with insufficient analysis: JOOD performance ranges 6.4% (LLaVA-1.5-7B) to 0.0% (LLaVA-OneVision)—no explanation. Model-specific parameters (Sb: 0.522-0.843, α: 9.6-29.3, Table 3) indicate significant per-model tuning, limiting claimed generalizability

Minimal calibration data and arbitrary risk function: Only 100 samples for calibrating Sb and α. Sigmoid risk mapping (Eq. 4) lacks theoretical justification. Figure 6 shows overlapping safe/unsafe distributions—sigmoid reliability questionable for ambiguous queries

Unsafe prototypes limited scope: Built from only 50 GPT-4 text queries (Fig. 8) focusing on instruction harms. Robustness to other harm types unexplored. Unclear whether prototypes generalize across jailbreak strategies

Insufficient failure analysis: VAA achieves 14.3% ASR—adversarial attacks remain effective. No analysis of failure modes or which attack types are hardest to defend against. No evaluation against adaptive attacks targeting MoRAS specifically

Design choices lack justification: Why N=3 tokens for risk evaluation vs. other values? Why exponential weighting over other schemes? Why sigmoid function specifically? Refusal vector comparison (Table 7) potentially unfair—different unsafe prototype sources

Over-refusal trade-off not fully addressed: Table 9 shows 3.2-4.3% increase in over-refusals on XSTest/OR-Bench. No user studies, preference data, or discussion of acceptability of this trade-off for practical deployment

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clear demonstration via attention maps and FDR analysis that MLLMs fail to allocate sufficient attention to safety-critical visual regions
Comprehensive experimental validation: 5 MLLM architectures, 5 safety benchmarks (SPA-VL, FigStep, MM-Safety, JOOD, VAA), 4 utility benchmarks; consistent ~19.4% average ASR reduction
Significant practical efficiency gains: 126.6× pre-deployment overhead reduction and 1.6× faster inference throughput compared to baselines
Thorough experimental analysis: Extensive ablations (Tables 2, 12), hyperparameter sensitivity studies, robustness across calibration sources, qualitative results with varying steering strengths
Strong generalization: Robust across diverse jailbreak types, MLLM architectures, and calibration dataset sources; works on both object-based and typographic attacks
Query-specific refusal vectors (Eq. 9) well-validated empirically (Table 7) vs. prior global formulations; clear three-stage pipeline design
High reproducibility: Algorithm 1 pseudocode, detailed implementation details, visual context prompts, and hyperparameters provided; over-refusal analysis included
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Visual context generation is straightforward; activation steering builds directly on prior work [23]; risk-adaptive scaling is intuitive but incremental. Primary contribution is problem identification plus combining existing techniques

Theoretical justification gaps: (1) Unclear why reformulated query visual contexts improve steering on original query activations; (2) FDR as proxy for safety lacks rigorous connection; (3) why cosine similarity to prototypes is appropriate metric not justified; (4) assumption that refusal behavior concentrates in first N tokens validated only empirically

Evaluation methodology concerns: (1) ASR uses MD-Judge-v0.2-Internlm2 without bias/correlation analysis; (2) some benchmarks small (FigStep 500 queries); (3) unclear how visual perturbations interact with visual context generation; (4) over-refusal increases non-negligible (3.2% XSTest, 4.3% OR-Bench)

Calibration dependency and data efficiency claims: (1) 150 calibration samples still required (not truly few-shot); (2) prototype diversity/representativeness of 50 GPT-4 queries not analyzed; (3) model-specific parameters highly variable (Sb ∈ [0.52, 0.84], α ∈ [9.6, 29.3]); (4) non-trivial calibration source variance (Table 6, up to 0.4% ASR difference)

Comparison fairness: Pre-deployment overhead comparison conflates different methodologies—MoRAS computes prototypes vs. ASTRA trains adversarial images vs. AutoSteer trains classifiers. Different baselines may be suboptimally tuned (Sec. 13 shows hyperparameter sensitivity). Some baselines (CoCA, ECSO) have zero pre-deployment overhead by design

Attention analysis limitations: (1) FDR setup with identical text and different images is artificial scenario; (2) attention extraction (Eq. 7) averaging over top-3 heads is arbitrary—no sensitivity analysis; (3) attention patterns' generality across architectures unclear; (4) visual context quality (accuracy, completeness) not analyzed

Missing failure case analysis: No systematic study of when method fails (MoRAS still 7.6% ASR on SPA-VL); no characterization of attack properties that resist the defense; no adversarial evaluation assuming attackers know about visual context or prototypes

Scalability and future-proofing: (1) All experiments on 7B-13B models; scaling to 70B+ unclear; (2) prototypes fixed at inference—how to handle novel post-deployment attacks?; (3) additional forward passes for visual context generation; full computational cost not fully itemized

Visual context generation bias: Using the model's own descriptions could introduce bias if model struggles with threatening objects; alternative visual description methods not explored; potential circularity in prompt wording ('safety-critical context')

Incomplete design justification: Exponential weighting (γ=0.3) lacks principled motivation beyond empirical validation; sigmoid risk mapping (Eq. 4) not compared to learned alternatives; generalization across calibration set mismatches (e.g., calibrated SPA-VL, tested JOOD) not evaluated
